documents: Stewart et al. 2022, Global Biogeochemical Cycles 36, e2022GB007351 (published paper, PDF, 16 pages)

entry.evidence: Is the dilution pattern (decreasing concentrations with increasing discharge) of DIC export universal?

steps.action: Set out the literature rivals for what controls DIC concentrations: lithology (carbonate weathering) versus climate and vegetation (soil respiration).
steps.quote: It has remained equivocal whether lithology or climate primarily controls DIC concentrations.

steps.action: Adopted the Shallow and Deep Hypothesis from earlier work, including the authors' own, as the explanation of dilution CQ patterns: DIC-rich groundwater at low flow, DIC-poor soil water at high flow.
steps.quote: This explanation, referred to as the Shallow and Deep Hypothesis

steps.action: Posed two continental-scale questions: whether DIC dilution is universal, and what drives short-term (weather) and long-term (climate) DIC responses.
steps.quote: [...] drivers of short-term DIC response to weather and long-term response to climate at the continental scale?

steps.action: Collated USGS river chemistry, discharge, climate and watershed attributes from CAMELS-Chem for more than 100 minimally impacted rivers with at least 10 coincident discharge, pH and HCO3- measurements.
steps.quote: This work used data from a new data set, CAMELS-Chem

steps.action: Checked that the sampled discharges span the interquartile range of the full discharge record, so that mean concentrations are not biased toward extreme flows.
steps.quote: The range of discharge measurements with coincident concentrations typically fell between the first and third quartiles of the full discharge range

steps.action: Computed DIC from measured pH and bicarbonate using carbonate equilibrium constants, and computed arithmetic-mean Cm and mean specific discharge Qm per site.
steps.quote: The calculation of DIC concentration is based on pH and bicarbonate concentrations at individual sites.

steps.action: Tailored the steady-state watershed reactor model (Li et al., 2022) with a Transition State Theory rate law to derive Cm = CeqR0/(QmCeq+R0) and its power-law limit Cm = AQm^B.
steps.quote: Here, we tailor the equations and solutions specifically for DIC.

steps.action: Checked the model premise of negligible external input by computing rainfall DIC from Henry's law and comparing it with reaction-generated DIC.
steps.quote: one to two orders of magnitude lower than DIC generated via reactions in soils and rocks

steps.action: Fitted power-law CQ relationships at each of 102 sites; 93 show dilution (b<0), and the nine flushing sites are mostly data-poor Gulf Coast sites.
steps.quote: 93 show dilution patterns

steps.action: Regressed CQ slope b against more than 50 watershed characteristics and found no significant correlation (also reported in Methods, p. 3).
steps.quote: Linear regression analysis between b and watershed characteristics, however, did not reveal strong correlations

steps.action: Derived the expectation that, if the shallow and deep hypothesis holds for DIC, soil CO2 and DIC should increase with depth.
steps.quote: If the shallow and deep hypothesis holds true for DIC, the near-universal dilution patterns would indicate increasing DIC or soil CO2 concentrations with depth.

steps.action: Compiled soil CO2 depth profiles (and DIC at Sleepers River) from six intensively measured CZO, LTER and USGS sites.
steps.quote: we compiled depth profiles from a few intensively measured sites

steps.action: Compared the profiles with the expectation: soil CO2 and DIC increase with depth at all six sites, which the authors read as confirming the hypothesis.
steps.quote: The collated soil CO2 and DIC concentration depth profiles confirm shallow and deep hypothesis

steps.action: Mapped aridity, Qm and Cm across the US and placed sites on the Budyko curve; higher Cm occurs in arid, water-limited sites.
steps.quote: Higher DIC concentrations occur under arid climates with high aridity index values.

steps.action: Compared cross-site Cm versus Qm data with reactor-model prediction curves for several Ceq and R0 pairs (Figure 3e-f).
steps.quote: The CmQm data follow the prediction lines from these equations, validating this theoretical prediction.

steps.action: Inferred a threshold discharge near 200 mm/yr and arid-climate Ceq of about 4 to 20 mM, attributed to pedogenic carbonate thermodynamics.
steps.quote: The data and model indicate a threshold discharge around 200 mm/ [...]

steps.action: Compared the threshold with published thresholds of 150 to 200 mm/yr for bicarbonate and geogenic solutes.
steps.quote: This threshold value is similar to the thresholds of 150–200 mm/yr identified for bicarbonate and geogenic solutes in the literature

steps.action: Examined rival controls: highlighted high-LAI and carbonate-rich sites, and regressed Cm on more than 50 characteristics; only carbonate fraction correlated (R2 = 0.58), so it was read as a secondary control.
steps.quote: none of the watershed characteristics, however, showed a significant correlation except for the fraction of carbonate rocks

steps.action: Computed riverine pCO2 from pH, bicarbonate and Henry's law, and related it to Cm, mean pH and Qm (Figure 4).
steps.quote: The concentrations of pCO2, an indicator of CO2 evasion potential, were calculated using pH, concentration of bicarbonate, and Henry's law

steps.action: Kept the shallow and deep framework, linking soil CO2 depth profiles and flow paths, as the driver of instantaneous DIC response (Figure 5).
steps.quote: The near-universal export patterns of DIC and soil CO2 depth profiles piece together a conceptual framework

steps.action: Rejected lithology as the primary driver of long-term mean DIC in favour of climate, keeping carbonate abundance as secondary.
steps.quote: CmQm relationships indicate the predominant controls of climate on mean DIC, instead of lithology.

steps.action: Kept the headline claim of distinct drivers: subsurface CO2 (from below) for short-term C, climate (from above) for long-term Cm.
steps.quote: baseline mean concentration is regulated by climate (from above)

end.claim: Daily-to-seasonal riverine DIC variations are controlled by subsurface CO2 depth distribution and flow paths, whereas long-term mean DIC is regulated by climate (production versus export), not primarily by lithology.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing cross-site Cm-Qm data with the steady-state reactor-model curves is what supports climate (export versus production) as the regulator of mean DIC.

gates.evidence: The shallow and deep hypothesis directed the compilation of depth profiles (' [...] idea, we compiled depth profiles', p. 7), but the main river data were collated without a hypothesis. The profiles could have failed to increase with depth, but they come from only six sites. The model curves use Ceq and R0 values chosen to bracket the data, with no stated fit or failure criterion (inference). No hypothesis, analysis or threshold is stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Transition State Theory rate law with a thermodynamic limit
Carbonate equilibrium constants and Henry's law to compute DIC and pCO2
Watershed as a well-mixed reactor (reactor versus transporter)

novelty_claims.quote: This work used data from a new data set, CAMELS-Chem

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims and their statuses: the near-universal dilution pattern is regularity_in_range (93 of 102 sites, b from -0.50 to 0.24); the threshold of about 200 mm/yr and Ceq of 4 to 20 mM are estimates given without uncertainty (estimate_with_resolution at best, weakly characterized); lithology as secondary rests on a regression; the pCO2 and pH patterns are descriptive. The shallow and deep confirmation rests on six sites whose profiles are not co-located with the >100 rivers, and the authors note colocated data are 'typically unavailable'. The model curves appear to be drawn for selected Ceq and R0 pairs rather than fitted; no goodness of fit is reported (inference). The regression reports carbonate fraction as the only significant correlate of Cm (R2 = 0.58), yet the paper concludes climate is primary; no regression on Qm or aridity is reported in comparable terms, a tension the text does not resolve (inference). No robustness tests are reported: flux-weighted versus arithmetic means, record length, or exclusion of data-poor flushing sites. The flushing classification is noted as weak but not tested. Two sites were excluded from the statistics for abnormal b. The Figure 4 caption says mean pH is 'high' at high discharge, which contradicts the text (likely a typo). The order of work (whether the hypothesis preceded the data analysis) cannot be read from the paper.

disagreements.target: Common perception that lithology drives DIC concentrations (Bluth & Kump, 1994; Doctor et al., 2008; Marx et al., 2017; van [...]
disagreements.support: Cross-site Cm-Qm relationships and the reactor-model curves point to climate as the primary control, with carbonate fraction secondary.
disagreements.quote: [...] perception that highlights lithology as the driver of DIC concentrations

disagreements.target: Commonly used flux-normalized mean concentrations (Godsey et al., 2019; Ibarra et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: Argues that flux weighting over-weights high-discharge samples and biases means when sampling is inconsistent across sites; no quantitative comparison is shown.
disagreements.quote: [...] to use the arithmetic mean instead of the commonly used flux-normalized mean concentrations

alternatives_considered.reason: Equal weight to every data point; flux weighting biases toward high discharge when sampling timing is inconsistent

alternatives_considered.chosen: Include all sites with at least 10 coincident C-Q-pH measurements
alternatives_considered.reason: Scarcity of water chemistry data; include as many sites as possible

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude Sopchoppy River and Blackwater River from the statistical analyses
alternatives_considered.reason: Abnormal CQ power-law slope b values

alternatives_considered.chosen: Soil CO2 depth profiles (DIC only at Sleepers River)
alternatives_considered.reason: Soil CO2 measurements more abundant at intensively measured sites

alternatives_considered.chosen: Power-law moisture dependence f(Sw) = Sw^n and Wittenberg storage-discharge relation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Storage-discharge relationships in various forms (Kirchner, 2009); optimum-type moisture functions
alternatives_considered.reason: Watershed mean soil moisture rarely exceeds 0.5, below the respiration optimum
